messages.subject: MCEM for missing obs data
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I just started using NIMBLE, and find it very useful. I tried BUGS/JAGS/Stan but I think the use of MCMC samplers  inside R is a huge advantage. During the past week, I found that NIMBLE is much much faster than my own C++ MCMC algorithm - not surprising at all. Using NIMBLE compiler, I see the path way to make normal R codes faster via C++. I am also glad this is happening at Berkeley.

Reading the manual, the MCEM function came to my attention because I was struggling with the convergence problem of EM, very sensitive to the initial values. I started with the example in the NIMBLE manual and built a simple (but useful) model as follows. It estimates the values somewhat higher or lower than what I provided in the data. I wonder why this is the case.

More importantly, I would like to know how I can implement the model with missing obs. In the traditional EM, I use the obs matrix, which is just a scalar "phi" in my model below, to indicate whether there are missing values.

I would appreciate any ideas or help.

Thank you very much.

Seongeun

# Model
bgModelCode <- nimbleCode({
x[1] ~ dnorm(mu_0, 1)
y[1] ~ dnorm(x[1], 1)
for(i in 2:t){

 x[i] ~ dnorm(phi*x[i-1] + d, 1)
y[i] ~ dnorm(x[i], 1)

}
phi ~ dnorm(1, .5)
d ~ dnorm(1, .5)
mu_0 ~ dnorm(1, .5)
})

# some made-up data, random walk with a drift

t = 25; mu_0 = 1
x = rnorm(1 ,mu_0, 1)
y = rnorm(1, x, 1)
phi = 1; d = 1
for(i in 2:t){
x[i] = rnorm(1, phi*x[i-1] + d, 1)
y[i] = rnorm(1, x[i], 1)
}

# Run MCEM to get params
myMCEM <- buildMCEM(model = rModel,
latentNodes = 'x',
burnIn = 100,
mcmcControl = list(adaptInterval = 10),
boxConstraints = list( list( c('phi', 'd', 'mu_0'),
limits = c(0, 100) ) ),
buffer = 1e-6)
res = myMCEM(maxit = 50, m1 = 250, m2 = 500)

> res
      phi         d      mu_0
0.9638035 1.5226775 0.6414609

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the update.  I was just in the midst of responding to your previous message.

Thanks for this question and glad to hear NIMBLE looks useful for you.

I may not be following what you want to achieve.  It looks like you are treating all values of ‘x’ as missing, and that seems reasonable.  Do you want some values of x[i] to be missing and some to be observed?  MCEM is used in lots of fields with context-specific details, so I don’t know what you mean by “In the traditional EM, I use the obs matrix, which is just the scalar “phi”.”  To me phi looks like the autocorrelation of latent state dynamics.

In general in NIMBLE, any values of x[i] that are provided as NA will be treated as missing data.  For buildMCEM, the missing data nodes are provided via the latentNodes argument.  If you provide ‘x’, it will treat all of x as missing.  But if ‘x’ has been provided as non-NA data, I am not completely sure that would work; I’d have to check, which I will wait to do until I am sure what you want to do.  If you want to provide only some elements of x in the latentNodes argument, you could use rModel$expandNodeNames(‘x’) and then subset that vector as needed.

Does that help?  Otherwise can you say more clearly what you want to be missing data?

Perry

messages.subject: Re: MCEM for missing obs data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Seongeun,

Thanks for the further explanation.  So you want to use MCEM to estimate phi, d, and mu_0 with some values of y missing.  I think it should work to provide missing values of y as NA and then include the names of those elements of y in the latentNodes argument to buildMCEM.  For example you might have latentNodes = c(rModel$expandNodeNames(‘x’), ‘y[10]’, ‘y[20]’), if y[10] and y[20] are the missing data nodes.  You might be able to extract the missing data nodes programmatically using rModel$getNodeNames(endOnly = TRUE), since those represent what we call “end” nodes (they have no stochastic dependencies).  Similarly you could identify the x nodes as rModel$getNodeNames(latentOnly = TRUE).  See help(modelBaseClass) for more options about querying the model.

I should mention we have an improved version of MCEM in a development branch, which provides more control over algorithm choices.    Let me know if you’d like to get involved as a beta tester for that!

Perry

messages.body_plain:
For better or for worse, this is a known error where the NIMBLE MCMC is finding the "slice" function from another package you have loaded (perhaps package "bbmle"?  If not that, there are other possibilities...)

This has already been fixed on the development branch of NIMBLE.  You can build and install that version locally:
> library(devtools)
> install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "devel", subdir = "packages/nimble")
> library(nimble)

Another comment about your code: Your call (which produced the error)

Cmcmc <- buildMCMC(ModSpec)

implies a bit of a misnomer, in that the buildMCMC() command will create an *R* version of the MCMC algorithm -- also executable, although very slow.  To get a compiled (C++) version of the algorithm, you'd then have to call compileNimble.  So the usual flow (and more correct variable names) would be:

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(ModSpec)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

Let me know how this works for you.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
I think it should work ok.

The only potential interaction I’d worry about is where the generated C++ and then compiled .o and .so files are placed.  By default they are placed in R’s automatically created temporary directory (which you can find by tempdir() ).  I think each R session should make a distinct temporary directory even if they are sharing a file system, so you should be ok.

If you are providing a dirName argument to compileNimble (which would tell it where you want it to put the C++ and related files), then it could be a problem if they two processes share a file system and attempt to use the same directory for their nimble compilation.

But let us know if you encounter any other problem I’m not anticipating.

Perry

messages.subject: version 0.5-1 of NIMBLE released
messages.body_plain:
Dear nimble-users and nimble-announce,

We're pleased to announce that we've released version 0.5-1 of NIMBLE at
R-nimble.org.

Version 0.5-1 is officially a minor release but it actually has quite
a bit going on, particularly in terms of new and improved algorithms.
Highlights include:
- the addition of a variety of sequential Monte Carlo (aka particle
filtering) algorithms, including particle MCMC samplers for use within
an MCMC (thanks to our 2015 Google Summer of Code student, Nick
Michaud)
- a greatly improved MCEM algorithm with an automated convergence and
stopping criterion (also thanks to Nick)
- new syntax for declaring multivariate variables in the NIMBLE DSL,
namely numeric(), integer(), matrix(), and array(), with declare() now
deprecated,
- addition of the multivariate-t distribution for use in BUGS and DSL
code (thanks to a Berkeley masters student, Peter Sujan),
- a new binary MCMC sampler for discrete 0/1 nodes,
- addition of functionality to our random walk sampler to allow
sampling on the log scale and use of reflection,
- more flexible use of forwardsolve(), backsolve(), and solve(),
including use in BUGS code, and
- some speed improvements in building and compiling models and algorithms.

More details on the NIMBLE web page and the NEWS file of the package.

We've had a bit of a hiccup in terms of getting on CRAN (some issues with
linking shared object files in a robust way when building package binaries)
but anticipate that happening in June, in addition to another release
that should bring
some major improvements in the speed of building and compiling models
with many nodes.

 - Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team
